rejections.text: The polling data suggests a more complicated picture than a guaranteed victory for Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, because while his popularity is undeniable across Cairo, there remains significant economic anxiety among urban youth and working-class families who might ultimately support a civilian alternative like Hamdeen Sabahi if economic conditions continue to deteriorate in the coming months ahead of the vote.

reasons.detail: In February 2014, following the military-backed ouster of Morsi, Sisi's immense popularity and the near-certainty of his presidential victory were widely recognized, while Hamdeen Sabahi was never viewed as a viable threat to defeat him in actual polling data at the time.

rejections.text: It depends largely on how the Muslim Brotherhood and its remaining underground networks decide to respond to the electoral process. If they mount a concerted boycott or launch widespread disruptions, the security apparatus might feel compelled to impose even tighter restrictions, which could paradoxically undermine the legitimacy of Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's eventual presidency and alienate crucial moderate voters in places like Alexandria and Giza.

reasons.detail: Answer 1 addresses whether Sisi will win and the implications for democracy, while Answer 2 discusses how the Muslim Brotherhood's response and security measures might affect the legitimacy of his presidency.

texts: Well, that's completely correct. Certainly no verdict, no ruling would have satisfied all Egyptians. At the same time, people were, as you know, intensely fixated on the court proceedings, the idea that Mr. Mubarak who had ruled the country for 29.5 years as an authoritarian dictator, really, was in a cage put on trial, held accountable, was something that was mesmerizing. At the same time, you know, this shows us that the Egyptian revolution has not been completely successful. We know, for example, that the prosecutors were not helped with -- did not have full cooperation from the Ministry of Interior that could have supplied more hard evidence as to what actually happened during those 18 days, whether orders were given or not, what the minister of interior said to Mr. Mubarak, and so on. There was reluctance to cooperate with the prosecution to defend their own. So clearly this also shows that not enough change has happened in Egypt in the 16 months since the revolution.

Well, there's been a great deal of speculation how one particular verdict or another would impact the elections. If Mr. Mubarak was acquitted there's no question that would have angered millions of Egyptians and that they would have more likely then voted in favor of the Muslim Brotherhood anti-regime figure. This verdict is a kind of, as you said, glass half full, glass half empty situation. So the regime candidate, Mr. Mubarak's last prime minister, who was in the runoff, can say, look, the revolution has succeeded. Mr. Mubarak is now in jail for the rest of his life, and let's move on, and elect me as president. As I mentioned, I think many Egyptians, those who favored change, who decried corruption and authoritarianism are unsatisfied with this verdict and are likely, I would think, to be skeptical at the very least about Ahmed Shafi, Mr. Mubarak's last prime minister who is running in elections against the Muslim Brotherhood candidate.

position_check.why: Both versions express the exact same viewpoint that Sisi's candidacy will cause other candidates to withdraw and that having a military general as president does not bode well for Egyptian democracy after sixty years of military rule.
